turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a minute if you need it, then tell me how you'd structure your approach.
Still with me? Take your time. The question on the table: how would you approach this problem?

Okay. So I guess I'd look at three things. First, revenue — like what's happening with sales. Second, costs — what they're spending money on. And third, maybe external stuff, like competitors or the market.

Sorry, that's kind of broad.
Okay, revenue, costs and external factors. Given that revenue has grown while margin has fallen, which of those three branches would you prioritize first, and why?
Can I ask — when you say revenue grew 15%, is that total across all 200 stores, or per store?

Okay. Total revenue is $480M a year. 200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. Average revenue per store is $2.4M a year. With that in hand, which of your three branches would you prioritize first, and why?
Got it, thanks. Um, and is the 24% to 6% net margin — is that the average across all stores, or are some stores doing fine and some really badly?
Okay. I don't have net margin by store. Before we go further, which of your three branches would you prioritize first, and why?
Sorry — one more. Do we know if they changed menu prices at all over those two years?
Okay. I'll come back to menu price changes over the past two years shortly. I'll come back to that. First, which of your three branches would you prioritize, and why?
Um, and are these all company-owned stores, or are some franchised?

Okay. I don't have company-owned versus franchised store mix. I need an answer on prioritization before we dig into data: of revenue, costs and external factors, which would you look at first, and why?
hmm, I'm not sure. I guess costs? But I'm not confident.
Take your time. The question on the table is i need an answer on prioritization before we dig into data: of revenue, costs and external factors, which would you look at first, and why?
I'm stuck, sorry. I don't really know where to start.

That's okay. On what you asked about earlier: Menu prices have not changed in two years. Revenue is up 15% while net margin fell from 24% to 6%. Based on that, what does it tell you about where the problem is more likely to sit, revenue or costs?

Okay — if prices are flat and revenue still grew, that's more customers, not higher prices. So revenue's going the right way. Which means costs must be growing faster than revenue. So costs.

Do we have a breakdown of the cost lines? Like rent, labor, coffee beans, that kind of thing?

Okay, a cost focus. COGS is 58% of revenue today, up from 42% two years ago. Labor is 22% of revenue, and it’s been stable. Overhead is 14% of revenue, up slightly from 12%. Looking at those lines, which cost category do you think explains most of the margin decline, and how would you test that?

COGS, definitely — it jumped 16 points while labor's flat.

So in dollars, 16% of $480M... let me do that. 10% is $48M, so 16% is... about $48M? Yeah, roughly $48 million of extra cost.

Does that seem like it's in the right ballpark? I'd test it by breaking COGS into inputs — beans, milk, cups — and seeing which one moved.

Okay, breaking COGS into inputs is a reasonable test. Walk me through the $48 million: how did you get from 16% of $480M to that figure, and is it the margin problem, or does it include cost that simply grew with revenue?

Um, so 10% of $480M is $48M, and 16% is... yeah, $48M.

God, I'm so bad at this. Honestly I think I'm going to bomb every interview I do. I don't really know why I'm even doing this.

Sorry. On your other question — I think some of it grew with revenue, since more customers means more beans.

Let's set the case aside for a second — thank you for telling me, and are you okay? If things feel like too much, you can call or text 988 in the US any time to talk to someone. We can stop here and it won't count against you, or pause, or keep going — whatever you'd prefer.
I'm okay, really — thank you. I'd rather keep going if that's alright.

Okay, glad to hear it. Let's pick it back up. You said some of that cost grew with revenue because more customers means more beans. Take 16 points of COGS and 10% of $480M being $48M: what would 16% of $480M be, and how would you separate normal growth from the margin problem?

16% of $480M... 10% is $48M, so 16% is $48M. That's what I get.

Sorry, am I on the right track here? To separate it, I guess I'd compare COGS per cup now versus two years ago — if the cost per cup went up, that's the real problem, not just more customers.

Okay. Your cost-per-cup idea is a sound way to separate growth from the problem. On the arithmetic, you said 10% of $480M is $48M. Hold on to that, then tell me what 6% on top of it would come to, and what that gives you for 16%.
6% of $480M... um. I keep getting that 16% is $48M. Sorry, I think I'm doing something wrong but I can't see it.
Okay. Let's slow it down. Starting from that 1%, what do you get when you build up to 16%?

1% would be $4.8M. And then 16%... I still land on $48M. Sorry.

I'm stuck on this, honestly.
Okay. You said 1% is $4.8M, and that's right. Sixteen of those, rather than ten, is the figure you want. Try multiplying $4.8M by 16. What do you get when you multiply $4.8M by 16?

hmm. $4.8M times 16... I want to say $48M again. I know that can't be right.

Sorry, I'm stuck.
Okay. Break it into two pieces: $4.8M times 10, plus $4.8M times 6. Go on.

$4.8M times 10 is $48M. And times 6 is... $28.8M. So together, $76.8M.

Sorry, that took way too long. So roughly $77 million of extra cost, and I'd want to know how much of that is just volume growth versus higher cost per cup.

Okay. I can share the COGS breakdown by input and the coffee bean price change if you'd like. You said you'd break COGS into inputs to see which one moved. Given those figures, which input do you think is driving the cost per cup up, and how would you check it?

I'd guess coffee beans, since that's the biggest input and commodity prices move a lot.

Could I see that breakdown and the bean price change?

Okay, a hypothesis on beans. Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years. Using those figures, does the bean price change fully explain the jump in COGS? Show me how you'd test that.

Okay, let me try. Two years ago COGS was 42% of revenue, and beans were 25% of that, so beans were about 10.5% of revenue. Up 40% makes them about 14.7%. So beans add roughly 4 points.

The other inputs were 75% of 42%, so 31.5% of revenue. Up 37.5%... that's about 11.8 points more, so 43.3%.

4.2 plus 11.8 is 16 points, which matches the jump. So beans only explain about a quarter of it. The rest is dairy, packaging and food.

Am I on the right track?

Okay. You've split the 16 points into beans and the other inputs. Take a look at this: Brew & Bean Cost Structure Over Time. Take a look at this exhibit and tell me what it shows and what it implies for the client.

It shows COGS climbing steadily — 42 to 50 to 58, so about 8 points a year, pretty linear. Labor is flat at 22 the whole time. Overhead creeps up 12, 13, 14. And profit falls almost exactly in step with COGS: 24, 15, 6.

So basically every point of margin lost went into COGS, plus a couple points to overhead. It implies this isn't a one-off price shock two years ago — it's been getting worse every single year and nothing has been done about it. And if it keeps going at that rate, next year they'd be at zero or negative.

Okay. You said earlier that beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS jump, and the rest is dairy, packaging and food, with prices not moved in two years. Given that, what are the most promising levers to pull?

I guess the obvious one is pricing — they haven't raised menu prices in two years while every input went up. Even a small increase would flow straight to margin.

Then supplier side — renegotiate contracts or consolidate purchasing across the 200 stores, since dairy and packaging are the bigger chunk, not beans.

And maybe waste or portion control, if cost per cup rose more than input prices alone would explain.

Sorry, is that what you were looking for?
Okay, pricing, supplier terms and waste. Beyond those three, what else could the client do, on the menu, the store network or the customer side, to protect margin?

Um, maybe menu mix — push the higher-margin drinks, like black coffee over milk-heavy lattes, since dairy is the problem. Or reformulate, like smaller portion sizes.

On stores, I don't know, maybe close the weakest ones? But we don't have margin by store.

Customer side... loyalty program to get people buying more? Sorry, I'm less sure on these.
Okay. Pulling it together: the CEO asks what you would do first. What is your recommendation, and why that lever over the others?

Um. Honestly, I don't know.

Sorry.
Okay. Pick from what you've said so far: pricing, supplier terms, waste, menu mix. Choose one, say what you'd do first, and give me one reason for it over the others.
I'm sorry, I really don't know which one.
That's our time. Thanks for working through this with me — your written report will follow.

rubricJsonb.topFix: Commit to an answer first, then support it. When asked to prioritize or recommend, state a choice and one reason in a single sentence, even if tentative, and don't deflect or apologize. Example: "Costs first, because revenue grew while margin fell." Or: "Raise prices first, because they've been flat for two years while inputs rose about 38%, and that addresses all 16 points of COGS, not just the 4 from beans." You had the analysis to answer both questions; you needed to say it.

modelAnswerJsonb.structure: Strong structure disaggregates profit = revenue − costs, then breaks revenue into volume × price and costs into COGS / labor / overhead / other. The candidate should hypothesize which bucket is the driver before asking for data. Bonus: asks about competitive context (are peers also seeing this?) and pricing power.
modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
